hops.title: Compare it: a menhaden eats like a kitchen strainer
hops.text: Grab a kitchen strainer when your child draws the menhaden card, and swish it through a bowl of water together. A menhaden eats a bit like that. It strains tiny floating plankton out of the Bay water. Striped bass and ospreys then eat the menhaden, so the sun's energy keeps moving along.

sources.citation: NOAA National Ocean Service, "What are phytoplankton?"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small school of silvery menhaden swims through sunlit green-tinted bay water dotted with tiny specks of plankton.
image.caption: A menhaden strains tiny floating plankton from the water, a bit like a kitchen strainer.

hops.title: Ask it: how many caterpillars does one chickadee nest need?
hops.text: Ask your child, "How many caterpillars do you think chickadee parents catch to raise one nest of babies?" Expect guesses like ten, fifty or a million. Cheer every guess, then share the real number: Carolina chickadees gather about 9,000 caterpillars for one nest. Then wonder together where all those caterpillars got their own food.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, "Bird, Pollinator, & Wildlife Habitat Not Just for National Parks Anymore"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small black-capped chickadee perches on a sunlit oak branch holding a tiny green caterpillar near a nest hole.
image.caption: Carolina chickadee parents gather about 9,000 caterpillars to raise one nest of chicks.

hops.title: Point at it: bite marks on oak and maple leaves
hops.text: On your next walk, with you right beside your child, look at low oak or maple leaves with eyes only. Keep hands off insects and unknown plants. Spot small holes or notched edges? Many are bites from hungry insects, turning leaf into lunch. Oak trees alone feed more than 500 kinds of caterpillars.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, "Bird, Pollinator, & Wildlife Habitat Not Just for National Parks Anymore"

image.caption: Small holes and notched edges on oak leaves are often bites from hungry insects.

audio.title: Three playful ways to talk about food chains at home
audio.transcript: Hi there! Before you build the yarn web together, here are three easy ways to make those picture cards come alive, with no quiz feeling at all. First, when your child draws the menhaden card, pull a kitchen strainer out of the drawer and swish it through a bowl of water. A menhaden eats a bit like that. It strains tiny floating plankton out of the Bay water. Tiny floating algae use sunlight to make food. In fact, the ocean produces about half of the oxygen made on Earth, mostly thanks to tiny floating living things like these. Then striped bass and ospreys eat the menhaden, and the sun's energy keeps moving along. Second, try a guessing game about backyard birds. Ask your child how many caterpillars Carolina chickadee parents catch to raise just one nest of babies. Kids love tossing out wild numbers like ten or a million. Cheer every guess, then share the real answer: about nine thousand caterpillars, gathered over about sixteen days, for a single nest. Then wonder together where all those caterpillars got their own food. Third, on your next walk, stay right beside your child and look at the low leaves of an oak or a maple, eyes only, hands off insects and unknown plants. Spot little holes or notched edges? Many of those are bites from hungry insects. Oak trees, all the kinds together, feed more than five hundred kinds of caterpillars, so oaks are busy feeding a crowd. And a grasshopper can eat about half its body weight in green plants a day. Those nibbled leaves are your neighborhood food chain, right there in action. Have fun!
